renal cell carcinoma can occur after anaplastic rhabdomyo-sarcoma in a patient with a constitutional Tp53 germ line mutation, and that this association is likely coincidental rather than causal.
a patient with rhabdomyoblastoma developed renal cell carcinoma, which is a rare association.

the 2004 World Organization classification of tumours of the urinary system includes neuroblastoma-associated renal carcinoma and that we report the first case of rhabdomyo-sarcoma-associated renal carcinoma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the genetic factors involved in the pathogenesis of renal cell carcinoma, and the role of these factors in the development of this disease.
the development of an effective treatment for rhabdomyoblastoma.
the study of the role of the 2nd malignancies in the development of renal cell carcinoma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
rhabdomyoma-associated renal cell carcinomas are rare but do occur, and are likely to be associated with Tp53 mutation.

the 2nd malignancies in this child were not therapy-induced but were rather the result of a Tp53 germline mutation, which was present at the time of the 1st malignancy and thus likely contributed to its development.
the patient described herein is the first case of renal cell carcinoma associated with rhabdomyoma, and that the 2nd malignancies are most probably related to a constitutional Tp53 gene mutation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a germline mutation of Tp53 may be associated with the development of both embryonal rhabdomysarcoma and renal cell carcinoma.
a Tp53 mutation can be the link between rhabdomyo- sarcoma and renal cell carcinoma.
rhabdomyo-sarcoma-associated renal cancer is not a therapy-induced neoplasm but a manifestation of constitutional Tp53 germline mutation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
rhabdomyoblastic and neuroblastoma-associated renal tumors are not the only renal tumors that may be linked to a constitutional Tp53 germline mutation.
a pathogenic Tp53 mutation should be sought when a child presents with 2 or more cancers, even in the absence of family history of Li-Fraumenis syndrome.
a child with a 2nd malignancies should be evaluated for underlying predisposition.
